\chapter{Los --- The One That Does Not Add -s}
\label{ch:articles-los}
\hlchaptermodality{62}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say los libros and explain why the masculine plural article is not els.}

Complete ES-C44-los: produce los libros, give all four articles, and say why el does not simply take an -s.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[los libros]{los libros — \textquotedblleft{}the books\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C44-los}



\begin{quote}
Last chapter: \emph{la casa} $\to$ \emph{las casas}. Apply the same move to \emph{el libro} and say what you get, out loud, before reading on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: not els}]
If you said \emph{els libros}, you did exactly the right thing and Spanish did not.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{los} — \emph{the}, for more than one masculine thing.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{el libro} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{los} libro\textbf{s}} — the books.
\end{quote}

The noun behaved. The article did not: \emph{el} became \textbf{los}, not \emph{els}. Out of four articles this is the only one that changes more than its ending, and it is worth two minutes rather than a shrug.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
You have met this exact story before, three chapters ago, wearing different clothes.

\emph{El} is not a whole word that lost its way. It is a \textbf{worn-down} one: Latin \emph{illum} gave \emph{elo}, and \emph{elo} lost its final vowel to become \emph{el}. The plural came from \emph{illos} — and it did \textbf{not} lose that vowel. It kept it, dropped the front instead, and arrived as \textbf{los}.

So the pair is not \emph{el} + \emph{s}. It is two forms of one Latin word that wore down in two different directions:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
\textbf{masculine} & \emph{elo} $\to$ \textbf{el} & \emph{illos} $\to$ \textbf{los} \\
\textbf{feminine} & \emph{illam} $\to$ \textbf{la} & \emph{illas} $\to$ \textbf{las} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is the same shape as \emph{el} and \emph{lo}, which you met when the object pronouns started: the masculine forms lost a vowel where the feminine ones had none to lose. One sound change, showing up for the third time.

An \textquotedblleft{}irregular\textquotedblright{} article turns out to be a regular word that was worn down twice.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el libro\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}los libros\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el, la, los, las\textquotedblright{} — the whole set, in order
\end{itemize}
